plan_on.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics & Internal Energy

segments.title: System, Surroundings and the Three Types
segments.objective: Define system, surroundings, and classify systems as open, closed, or isolated.
segments.teaching_notes: Start by drawing an imaginary boundary around the part we care about. Explain that the system is what we study; the surroundings are everything else. Then introduce open, closed, and isolated systems with everyday examples: an open kadhai (matter and energy exchange), a sealed pressure cooker before whistle (energy only), and a thermos flask (neither). Emphasise that the type of system determines how energy and matter can be accounted for. Common pitfall: students confuse closed and isolated systems.
segments.board_content:
System = part of universe under study.
Surroundings = everything else.
Types:
• Open: exchanges matter & energy (e.g., boiling milk in open pan)
• Closed: exchanges energy only (e.g., sealed pressure cooker)
• Isolated: exchanges neither (e.g., ideal thermos flask)

checkpoint.question: Consider a perfectly sealed and insulated thermos flask containing hot tea. Classify this as a system: open, closed, or isolated?
checkpoint.model_answer: Isolated system because it exchanges neither matter nor energy with the surroundings.
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: isolated with justification. Partial: isolated without justification or closed with reasoning.
expected_misconceptions: confuses closed and isolated systems
thinks heat can pass through vacuum insulation
thinks matter exchange occurs through the lid

segments.title: State Functions, Path Functions and the First Law
segments.objective: Distinguish state and path functions, introduce internal energy (U), and state the first law with sign conventions.
segments.teaching_notes: Use the hill‑temple analogy: altitude gain (state function) depends only on start and end, while steps walked (path function) depends on route. Explain that U and H are state functions; q and w are path functions. Then introduce internal energy as total stored energy and give the first law: ΔU = q + w. Emphasise the IUPAC sign convention: q > 0 for heat absorbed, w > 0 for work done on the system. Note that for an isothermal ideal gas, ΔU = 0 because U depends only on T. Common misconception: treating q or w as state functions or saying a system 'contains heat'.
segments.board_content:
First Law: $\Delta U = q + w$
State functions: $U, H, T, P, V$ (depend only on end‑points)
Path functions: $q, w$ (depend on route)
For ideal gas, $U$ depends only on $T$: isothermal $\Rightarrow \Delta U = 0$

checkpoint.question: For the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, what is the change in internal energy (ΔU)? Briefly explain.
checkpoint.model_answer: ΔU = 0, because the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, and temperature remains constant.
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: states zero and mentions temperature dependence. Partial: states zero without explanation.
expected_misconceptions: thinks ΔU > 0 because work is done by the gas
confuses isothermal with adiabatic (q = 0)
believes internal energy depends on volume

segments.title: Expansion Work: Reversible vs Irreversible
segments.objective: Derive expressions for pressure–volume work and contrast reversible and irreversible paths.
segments.teaching_notes: Explain that work is done when a gas expands against an external pressure. For constant external pressure, w = –p_ext ΔV. Then show that if the expansion is carried out reversibly (p_ext ≈ p_int at every step), integration gives w = –nRT ln(V2/V1). Emphasise that reversible work is the maximum possible work for a given change, and that in a cyclic process ΔU = 0 so q = –w. Use physical reasoning: in a reversible process, the gas pushes against the largest possible opposing pressure. Common pitfalls: sign of w (negative for expansion), mixing up ln and log10, and forgetting that free expansion (p_ext = 0) gives w = 0.
segments.board_content:
Expansion work:
• Irreversible (constant $p_{ext}$): $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$
• Reversible isothermal (ideal gas): $w = -nRT \ln rac{V_2}{V_1}$
• Cyclic process: $\Delta U = 0 \Rightarrow q = -w$

checkpoint.question: Calculate the work done on the system when 1 mole of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 2.0 L to 6.0 L. (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: correct magnitude and negative sign. Partial: correct magnitude but wrong sign, or uses log10 instead of ln.
expected_misconceptions: forgets negative sign for expansion
uses log10 instead of natural log
uses wrong value of R (e.g., 0.0821 L·atm)

segments.title: Enthalpy and the ΔH–ΔU Connection
segments.objective: Define enthalpy, relate ΔH to ΔU, and introduce heat capacities.
segments.teaching_notes: Introduce enthalpy as H = U + PV, a state function useful for constant‑pressure processes. Derive ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV) and, for reactions involving ideal gases at constant T, ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT. Emphasise that only gaseous species count in Δn_g. Also mention that q_V = ΔU and q_P = ΔH, and give Mayer’s relation C_P – C_V = R for an ideal gas. Common traps: including solids/liquids in Δn_g, thinking ΔH and ΔU are always different, and forgetting that for isothermal ideal gas processes both ΔU and ΔH are zero.
segments.board_content:
Enthalpy: $H = U + PV$
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$  (ideal gases, constant $T$)
At constant $V$: $q_V = \Delta U$
At constant $P$: $q_P = \Delta H$
Ideal gas: $C_P - C_V = R$

checkpoint.question: For the reaction C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), what is the difference (ΔH – ΔU) at temperature T? Explain.
checkpoint.model_answer: Zero, because Δn_g = (moles of gaseous products) – (moles of gaseous reactants) = 1 – 1 = 0, and ΔH – ΔU = Δn_g RT.
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: zero and mentions Δn_g. Partial: zero without mentioning Δn_g.
expected_misconceptions: counts solid carbon as a gaseous species
thinks the difference is always RT
confuses sign of Δn_g (thinks it is 1)

wrapup_points: The system is the part we study; surroundings are everything else. Systems are classified by what crosses the boundary: open (matter + energy), closed (energy only), isolated (nothing).
State functions like U and H care only about the initial and final states; path functions like q and w depend on the route taken.
Expansion work depends on the path: reversible work is the maximum for a given change, and its formula is w = –nRT ln(V₂/V₁) for an isothermal ideal gas.
Enthalpy (H = U + PV) is tailored for constant‑pressure processes. The relation ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT helps convert between bomb‑calorimeter (ΔU) and open‑beaker (ΔH) measurements.

plan_off.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics & Internal Energy

segments.title: System, Surroundings, and Types of Systems
segments.objective: Define system, surroundings, and boundary; classify systems as open, closed, or isolated.
segments.teaching_notes: Start with the pressure cooker analogy: draw an imaginary boundary around the steam inside. The system is what we study; surroundings are everything else. Boundary can be real or imaginary. Three types: open (exchange matter and energy, like boiling milk), closed (exchange energy only, like sealed cooker), isolated (no exchange, like ideal thermos). Emphasize that classification depends on what crosses the boundary.
segments.board_content: $$\text{System} = \text{part under study}$$ $$\text{Surroundings} = \text{everything else}$$ $$\text{Open: matter + energy}$$ $$\text{Closed: energy only}$$ $$\text{Isolated: nothing}$$

checkpoint.question: A sealed pressure cooker on a stove is an example of which type of system?
checkpoint.model_answer: Closed system, because it can exchange energy (heat) but not matter (steam cannot escape).
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: closed system with reasoning about energy exchange but no matter exchange. Partial: just 'closed' without explanation.
expected_misconceptions: confuses closed with isolated
thinks any sealed container is isolated

segments.title: State Functions vs Path Functions
segments.objective: Distinguish state functions (like U, H) from path functions (like q, w) using the hill-temple analogy.
segments.teaching_notes: Use the trek to a hill temple: altitude gain depends only on start and end, not the path—that's a state function. Steps walked and water drunk depend on the route—path functions. Internal energy (U) and enthalpy (H) are state functions; heat (q) and work (w) are path functions. Stress that we can only measure changes in U, not absolute values. Mention that for a cyclic process, ΔU = 0 because U is a state function.
segments.board_content: $$\text{State function: depends only on state}$$ $$\text{Path function: depends on route}$$ $$U, H, T, P, V \text{ are state functions}$$ $$q, w \text{ are path functions}$$ $$\text{Cyclic process: } \Delta U = 0$$

checkpoint.question: Why is internal energy a state function while heat is not?
checkpoint.model_answer: Internal energy depends only on the current state (T, P, composition), not how the system got there. Heat is energy in transit and depends on the path taken between states.
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: explains that U depends on state variables, while heat is a process quantity. Partial: only says U is a state function without contrasting with heat.
expected_misconceptions: thinks heat is stored in the system
confuses state function with conserved quantity

segments.title: The First Law and Sign Convention
segments.objective: State the first law (ΔU = q + w) and apply the sign convention for heat and work.
segments.teaching_notes: Present the first law as energy conservation: energy entering as heat or work increases internal energy. Explain the IUPAC/NCERT sign convention: q > 0 if heat is absorbed by the system, w > 0 if work is done on the system. Use the memory aid 'on is plus, by is minus' for work. Walk through a simple example: if a system absorbs 250 J of heat and does 80 J of work, ΔU = 250 + (-80) = 170 J.
segments.board_content: $$\Delta U = q + w$$ $$q > 0: \text{heat absorbed}$$ $$w > 0: \text{work done ON system}$$ $$w < 0: \text{work done BY system}$$ $$\text{Example: } q = +250 \text{ J}, w = -80 \text{ J} \Rightarrow \Delta U = +170 \text{ J}$$

checkpoint.question: A system releases 120 J of heat and has 200 J of work done on it. What is ΔU?
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: +80 J with correct sign handling. Partial: correct magnitude but wrong sign.
expected_misconceptions: confuses sign of work done by vs on system
forgets to include sign of heat released

segments.title: Expansion Work: Reversible vs Irreversible
segments.objective: Calculate pressure-volume work for irreversible and reversible isothermal processes.
segments.teaching_notes: Explain that when a gas expands against an external pressure, work done on the system is w = -p_ext ΔV. For irreversible expansion against constant external pressure, use this directly. For reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, p_ext is adjusted to be only infinitesimally less than internal pressure, leading to w_rev = -nRT ln(V2/V1). Emphasize that reversible work is the maximum possible work. Contrast with free expansion (p_ext = 0, w = 0).
segments.board_content: $$w_{\text{irr}} = -p_{\text{ext}} \Delta V$$ $$w_{\text{rev}} = -nRT \ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$ $$\text{Reversible work is maximum}$$ $$\text{Free expansion: } w = 0$$

checkpoint.question: 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 290 K doubles its volume reversibly and isothermally. Calculate the work done. (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: -836 J (or close) with correct formula and sign. Partial: correct formula but arithmetic error.
expected_misconceptions: uses wrong sign for work
forgets to use natural log

segments.title: Enthalpy and the ΔH to ΔU Bridge
segments.objective: Define enthalpy (H = U + PV) and relate ΔH to ΔU using Δn_g RT.
segments.teaching_notes: Introduce enthalpy as a state function useful for constant pressure processes. Derive ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV). For ideal gases at constant T, Δ(PV) = Δn_g RT, where Δn_g = moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants. Emphasize that only gases count; solids and liquids are ignored. Show example: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), Δn_g = 2 - 4 = -2, so ΔH = ΔU - 2RT.
segments.board_content: $$H = U + PV$$ $$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$$ $$\Delta n_g = n_{\text{gas products}} - n_{\text{gas reactants}}$$ $$\text{Only gases count!}$$

checkpoint.question: For the reaction C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), what is ΔH - ΔU at temperature T?
checkpoint.model_answer: ΔH - ΔU = Δn_g RT. Δn_g = 1 - 1 = 0 (C is solid, ignored). So ΔH - ΔU = 0.
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: 0 with explanation that Δn_g = 0. Partial: correct answer but no reasoning.
expected_misconceptions: counts solid carbon in Δn_g
thinks ΔH - ΔU is always RT

segments.title: Applying the First Law: Isothermal and Cyclic Processes
segments.objective: Apply the first law to isothermal ideal gas processes and cyclic processes.
segments.teaching_notes: For an ideal gas, U and H depend only on T. So in any isothermal process, ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0. Then from first law, q = -w. For a cyclic process, the system returns to initial state, so ΔU = 0, and thus q_cycle = -w_cycle. Use JEE example: 2 mol ideal gas, isothermal reversible expansion from 5 L to 20 L at 300 K. Calculate w, q, ΔU, ΔH. w = -nRT ln(V2/V1) = -6.92 kJ, q = +6.92 kJ, ΔU = ΔH = 0.
segments.board_content: $$\text{Isothermal ideal gas: } \Delta U = 0, \Delta H = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow q = -w$$ $$\text{Cyclic process: } \Delta U = 0 \Rightarrow q_{\text{cycle}} = -w_{\text{cycle}}$$

checkpoint.question: In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the gas absorbs 500 J of heat. What is the work done by the gas?
checkpoint.model_answer: Since ΔU = 0, q = -w. Heat absorbed q = +500 J, so w = -500 J. Work done by the gas is 500 J.
checkpoint.rubric: Correct: 500 J with sign explanation. Partial: correct magnitude but wrong sign.
expected_misconceptions: thinks isothermal means q = 0
confuses sign of work done by gas

wrapup_points: System classification depends on what crosses the boundary: open (matter+energy), closed (energy only), isolated (nothing).
State functions (U, H) depend only on state; path functions (q, w) depend on the route.
First law: ΔU = q + w. Sign convention: heat absorbed and work done on system are positive.
Expansion work: irreversible w = -p_ext ΔV; reversible isothermal w = -nRT ln(V2/V1). Reversible work is maximum.
Enthalpy H = U + PV; ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT. Only gaseous moles count in Δn_g.
For isothermal ideal gas processes, ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0, so q = -w. For cyclic processes, ΔU = 0.
